opts.t: Advance an airway-exchange catheter through the displaced tube

Associated with lower emergence delirium risk.

More often paediatric moderate OSA.

questions.stem: In a patient with glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency (G6PD), the intravenous agent that should be avoided is

opts.why: Does not oxidatively damage red blood cells.
Not a standard G6PD haemolytic trigger.
Needs NADPH-dependent reduction and may provoke haemolysis or be ineffective in G6PD deficiency.
No oxidative mechanism.

opts.why: Baseline 10%; 20% relative reduction gives 8%; ARR=2%; NNT=1/0.02=50.
Confuses the 20% relative reduction with absolute risk reduction.
Would require ARR 10 percentage points.
Would require ARR 5 percentage points.

questions.expl: Relative risk reduction 20% is not a reduction from 10% to −10%; the absolute reduction is only 2 percentage points, yielding NNT 50.

questions.stem: The odds ratio is the measure of choice for a

opts.why: Cohort designs often support direct risk ratios.
Trials often permit risk ratios and risk differences.
Does not specifically require an odds ratio.
Odds ratio is estimable even when sampled by outcome, unlike incidence risks.

questions.expl: Case-control studies start by selecting cases and controls, so risk denominators are not known; exposure odds ratio measures association.

questions.stem: According to the categorisation system used in Australia and New Zealand for prescribing medicines safely in pregnancy, category X denotes drugs which are

opts.t: Medicines shown safe in all trimesters
opts.why: Corresponds to low-risk categories, not X.
Lack of data is not equivalent to category X.

opts.t: Medicines with a high risk of permanent fetal damage and contraindicated in pregnancy
opts.why: This is TGA category X.

opts.t: Medicines only associated with transient nausea
opts.why: Not the definition of high-risk category X.

questions.expl: Australian pregnancy category X is reserved for drugs with such a high risk of permanent damage to the fetus that they should not be used in pregnancy or potential pregnancy.

questions.stem: A patient is undergoing a posterior spinal fusion with somatosensory evoked potential (SSEP) monitoring. Ischaemia is suggested by

opts.why: Cord ischaemia reduces SSEP amplitude and delays conduction.
The reverse of ischaemic deterioration.
Amplitude typically falls.
Latency generally lengthens with impaired conduction.

questions.expl: Significant SSEP alert changes are amplitude decrease (often ≥50%) and latency increase (often ≥10%); assess anaesthesia, BP, temperature and technical factors.

questions.stem: The initial management for a seizure during an awake craniotomy is

opts.t: Irrigate cortical surface with ice-cold saline
opts.why: First intervention for focal seizure during awake functional mapping.
Slow-onset anticonvulsant is not the first rescue manoeuvre.

opts.why: May be required if ice-cold saline fails, but risks losing awake testing.

opts.t: Continue cortical stimulation to finish mapping
opts.why: Worsens the provoked seizure.

questions.expl: Mapping-induced seizures often terminate with stopping stimulation and iced saline irrigation; give small IV propofol/midazolam if persistent, secure airway as needed.

questions.stem: An absolute contraindication to skin prick testing for the diagnosis of allergies is

opts.why: Generally a caution/relative risk, not a universal absolute contraindication.
Invalidates skin-prick testing because the negative control becomes unreliable.
Suppresses wheal; test can be deferred until washout.
May alter risk management; usually relative consideration.

questions.expl: Skin prick results cannot be interpreted in severe dermographism; antihistamines, asthma, pregnancy or beta blockers are relative cautions depending on indication.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old man has undergone a right pneumonectomy for malignancy. Twelve hours postoperatively he suddenly develops profound hypotension and shock. Clinical examination reveals a raised central venous pressure. The most useful IMMEDIATE action would be to

opts.why: This is herniation, not typical tamponade from pericardial effusion.
Shock demands urgent correction.

opts.t: Wait for CT before haemodynamic stabilisation
opts.why: Urgent surgical review and stabilisation take priority.

opts.t: Place in left lateral decubitus position and urgently arrange surgical re-exploration
opts.why: With right-sided pneumonectomy cardiac herniation may improve when positioned away from the defect while preparing repair.

questions.expl: Post-pneumonectomy shock with raised CVP suggests cardiac herniation; reposition and urgently return to theatre to reduce the heart and repair defect. Imaging can aid diagnosis if stable.
questions.note: Exam/evidence qualification: Severe post-pneumonectomy instability needs immediate surgical assessment; the positioning manoeuvre is adjunctive, not definitive.

questions.stem: In cardiac surgery a low-normal central venous pressure and a low blood pressure with a hyperdynamic heart is suggestive of

opts.why: Low systemic vascular tone with low BP, low/normal filling pressures and hyperdynamic output is characteristic.
Would generally show impaired function and reduced output.
Shows impaired filling/high venous pressures.
Fixed outflow obstruction with non-hyperdynamic low-pressure state.

questions.expl: Vasoplegic shock is distributive, with low SVR and often hyperdynamic cardiac output after bypass or during inflammation.

questions.stem: Expected features of Guillain-Barré syndrome include

opts.why: Typical acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy presentation.
Unlike the characteristic hyporeflexia/areflexia.
Suggests central lesion.
Autonomic lability is an important GBS complication.

questions.expl: GBS is an acute peripheral neuropathy with progressive symmetrical weakness, reduced reflexes, possible cranial/respiratory involvement and dysautonomia.

questions.stem: In Australia and New Zealand, the proportion of blood donors who are cytomegalovirus (CMV) seropositive is

Far below recalled population estimates.
The recalled Australian/NZ donor range is roughly two-thirds to four-fifths.
Overstates universal exposure.

An unpleasant abnormal spontaneous sensation, often electric or burning.
Exaggerated pain to a normally painful stimulus.
Reduced sensation rather than unpleasant shooting sensation.

questions.expl: IASP dysaesthesia describes an unpleasant abnormal sensation, spontaneous or evoked; distinguishing stimulus is critical for allodynia/hyperalgesia.

Contributes at root/side of nose.
Contributes to lateral nose/ala.

Generally preferred non-NSAID analgesic.
No inherent lithium-retention mechanism.

questions.stem: You are planning to extubate a patient following airway surgery. The patient has FAILED the cuff-leak test when

opts.why: Suggests a patent space around the tube.

opts.why: Suggests airway oedema or narrowing and failed cuff-leak test.
Typically considered adequate leakage in common protocols.
Does not itself identify a failed cuff leak.

questions.expl: The cuff-leak test compares delivered vs exhaled volume or audible leak around a deflated tube; small/absent leak suggests risk of post-extubation stridor, but test has imperfect prediction.

questions.stem: Under the NEXUS criteria, requirements to clear the cervical spine of trauma patients without radiographic imaging include all of the following EXCEPT

Required by NEXUS.

opts.why: NEXUS clearance criteria are clinical and do not require radiography if all are satisfied.
Required by NEXUS (along with no distracting injury).

questions.expl: NEXUS low-risk criteria are: no midline tenderness, neurological deficit, intoxication, altered alertness or distracting injury. Imaging is not itself a clearance criterion.

questions.stem: You are called to recovery to review an 80-year-old woman after neck of femur fracture fixation performed under general anaesthesia with a fascia iliaca block. Unnecessary opioid and can worsen delirium.

questions.expl: First look for hypoxia, urinary retention, drugs, infection, hypoglycaemia and pain; non-pharmacological care first. Historical recalled exam answer: IV haloperidol for severe distress/risk, cautious ECG/QT review.

Ignores systematic difference.
Much greater separation than expected.

questions.stem: The antiemetic action of aprepitant is via receptors for

Target of droperidol/metoclopramide.
Target of promethazine/cyclizine.
Aprepitant antagonises NK1 receptors for substance P.

Permits hypotension and secondary cerebral injury.
Threshold applies to some patients aged 50–69, not 21.
May be reasonable individually but is above guideline minimum.

questions.stem: A patient you anaesthetised for a cervical fusion reports rapidly progressing unilateral visual loss commencing two days postoperatively. Fundoscopic examination reveals optic disc oedema. The most likely diagnosis is

Usually sudden severe visual loss with retinal pallor/cherry-red spot.
Disc oedema and delayed postoperative painless visual loss are compatible with AION.
Pain, corneal clouding, high IOP rather than isolated delayed optic-disc oedema.

questions.expl: Postoperative visual loss after prolonged spine surgery with swollen optic disc is most compatible with anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy; obtain urgent ophthalmology assessment.

questions.stem: A patient requiring an elective major joint replacement has had a recent stroke. The minimum recommended duration between the stroke and surgery is

opts.t: Three months as the minimum postponement

Still within the highest-risk interval after stroke.

opts.t: Twelve months as a universal minimum
opts.why: No universal 12-month minimum is established.

questions.note: Exam/evidence qualification: Minimum vs preferable timing is not equivalent. The exact 2023 original options are not published by ANZCA.

Too restrictive.

opts.why: Fourth consensus lowered threshold for multimodal prophylaxis.

questions.stem: A patient with an acute subarachnoid haemorrhage arrives in the emergency department. Her Glasgow Coma Scale score is 10 and she has no motor deficit. A CT brain shows diffuse subarachnoid haemorrhage with no localised areas of blood greater than 1mm thick, and no intracerebral or intraventricular blood. Her World Federation of Neurosurgical Societies (WFNS) grade of subarachnoid haemorrhage is

opts.why: GCS 15.
GCS 13–14 without deficit.
GCS 13–14 with deficit.
GCS 10–12 is WFNS grade IV irrespective of focal deficit.

questions.expl: WFNS is primarily GCS-based: I=15, II=13–14 no motor deficit, III=13–14 with deficit, IV=7–12, V=3–6.

Much longer than standard minimum, without individual indication.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department following a suspected amitriptyline overdose. She has a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 6 and her blood pressure is 90/46 mmHg. Her electrocardiogram is most likely to show

opts.why: Not typical sodium-channel toxicity.

opts.t: QRS widening, often with sinus tachycardia
opts.why: Sodium-channel blockade in TCA overdose produces broad QRS and terminal R in aVR.

opts.t: Isolated sinus bradycardia with normal intervals
opts.why: Anticholinergic effects more often cause tachycardia.
Not the characteristic primary toxidrome ECG finding.

questions.expl: TCA cardiotoxicity causes fast sodium-channel blockade: QRS prolongation, terminal R in aVR, hypotension and ventricular arrhythmia risk; sodium bicarbonate if QRS wide/instability.

questions.stem: Sacubitril use reduces the plasma levels of

opts.why: BNP is a neprilysin substrate and may rise during neprilysin inhibition.
Neprilysin inhibition increases BNP but NT-proBNP falls as wall stress improves with therapy.
Its degradation is inhibited, tending to increase levels.
Also a neprilysin substrate and may increase.

questions.expl: Sacubitril inhibits neprilysin; serial NT-proBNP is preferred to BNP for response assessment after initiation.

questions.stem: A drug that is NOT useful for the treatment of vasoplegic shock is

opts.why: V1-mediated vasoconstriction is useful.
Inhibits NO–cGMP vasodilatory signalling in selected refractory cases.
An inotrope/inodilator, not an effective primary vasoconstrictor for isolated low-SVR vasoplegic shock.
Can scavenge NO/H₂S and is used as rescue therapy in selected refractory vasoplegia.

questions.expl: For vasoplegia (high CO/low SVR), use vasoconstrictors including noradrenaline/vasopressin; inotropes such as dobutamine may worsen vasodilatation if cardiac output is already high.

questions.stem: A man has symptomatic carbon monoxide poisoning. His pulse oximetry (SpO2) and arterial blood gas (PaO2) would be expected to show

opts.why: PaO₂ commonly remains normal with isolated CO exposure.

opts.t: Normal SpO₂ rules out CO poisoning
opts.why: False: co-oximetry is required.

opts.t: Markedly elevated PaO₂ caused by CO itself
opts.why: CO reduces oxygen content, not alveolar O₂ transfer to dissolved PaO₂ in room air.

opts.t: Falsely normal/high SpO₂ with normal PaO₂
opts.why: Standard pulse oximetry cannot distinguish HbO₂ from carboxyHb; dissolved arterial oxygen can remain normal.

questions.expl: Suspect CO poisoning despite reassuring saturation; confirm with blood co-oximetry carboxyhaemoglobin, not standard pulse oximetry or PaO₂.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old woman presents for thrombectomy with left lower leg ischaemia. She has not received any medications since presentation and takes none at home. The sole abnormality on laboratory testing is an activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT) of 52 seconds. The most likely cause of the raised APTT is

opts.why: Paradoxically prolongs phospholipid-dependent aPTT in vitro while associated with thrombosis in vivo.
Produces bleeding tendency, not typically first thrombotic presentation.
Primarily prolongs PT, not aPTT.

opts.t: Normal physiological reaction to leg ischaemia
opts.why: Not a credible explanation for aPTT 52 seconds.

questions.expl: An arterial thrombosis with isolated prolonged aPTT and no anticoagulant exposure raises suspicion of lupus anticoagulant; confirm via mixing/DRVVT/APS testing.

questions.stem: A diagnosis of metabolic syndrome is NOT supported by

opts.why: A recognised diagnostic component.
A recognised diagnostic component.
Metabolic syndrome typically has LOW HDL cholesterol.
A recognised diagnostic component.

questions.expl: Metabolic syndrome criteria include abdominal obesity, high TG, low HDL, raised BP and hyperglycaemia (three of five).

questions.stem: The nerve most likely to be inadequately anaesthetised with an incomplete interscalene brachial plexus block is the

opts.why: Lower-trunk/medial-cord territory is often incompletely covered by an interscalene block.
Upper roots usually well covered.
Typically covered near the superior plexus.
Upper-root territory usually blocked.

questions.expl: Interscalene blockade most reliably covers C5–7 but often spares C8–T1, explaining poor ulnar/medial upper-limb coverage.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with alcohol-related cirrhosis is booked to undergo a transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPS) procedure. The calculation of his MELD-Na score to estimate his mortality risk requires all of the following EXCEPT

opts.why: Included as hepatic synthetic function measure.
Not included in MELD-Na calculation.
Included.
Both included.

questions.expl: MELD-Na uses bilirubin, creatinine, INR and serum sodium; albumin belongs to other prognostic systems (e.g. Child–Pugh).

questions.stem: Following the insertion of a peripherally inserted central catheter (PICC) into the cephalic vein in the upper arm, the patient complains of numbness in their forearm. It is likely that during insertion the operator has injured the

opts.why: Course not adjacent to usual cephalic vein insertion site.
Medial elbow course.
Not the primary cutaneous neighbour of cephalic vein.
Terminal sensory branch of musculocutaneous nerve lies adjacent to cephalic vein at lateral antecubital/upper arm.

questions.expl: Cephalic-vein PICC placement risks injury to lateral antebrachial cutaneous nerve with resulting lateral forearm paraesthesia.

opts.why: Common therapeutic duration; too early to terminate routinely.
May be within normal therapeutic seizure duration.
ECT seizure >120 seconds is prolonged and typically requires pharmacological termination.
Would delay treatment beyond usual safety protocol.

questions.expl: Many ECT protocols recommend terminating ongoing EEG/motor seizure at 120 s with anaesthetic agent/benzodiazepine; follow local protocol.

questions.stem: Of the following drugs, the LEAST likely to cause pulmonary vasodilation when used at low doses in patients with chronic pulmonary hypertension is

opts.why: Low-dose effects are mainly dopaminergic/β adrenergic; not a dependable selective pulmonary vasodilator.
PDE3 inhibitor lowers PVR and improves RV inotropy.
β agonist generally reduces PVR at low doses while improving output.
May lower PVR relative to SVR in some conditions.

questions.expl: In pulmonary hypertension avoid drugs that markedly increase pulmonary vascular resistance. Dopamine has unpredictable pulmonary effects and is least clearly pulmonary vasodilating among recalled choices.

questions.stem: According to the Revised Cardiac Risk Index, a 72-year-old male scheduled for a laparoscopic cholecystectomy with a history of hypertension, 20 pack-year history of smoking, type 2 diabetes requiring insulin and a previous stroke has a score of

opts.why: Counts only one of three factors.
Misses one of the major factors.
RCRI factors: intraperitoneal surgery, insulin-treated diabetes and prior stroke/TIA.
Hypertension/smoking are not RCRI variables.

questions.expl: Classic Lee RCRI uses high-risk surgery, IHD, heart failure, stroke/TIA, insulin use and creatinine >2 mg/dL (177 µmol/L). Laparoscopic cholecystectomy is classified as intraperitoneal in this historical scheme.

questions.stem: Cryoprecipitate contains coagulation factors

opts.t: Factors II, VII, IX and X
opts.why: Typical vitamin-K dependent PCC components, not cryoprecipitate.

opts.t: Factors I, VII, X and vWF
opts.why: VII and X are not enriched cryo components.

opts.t: Factors II, V, VII and IX
opts.why: Not the cryoprecipitate profile.

opts.t: Factors I, VIII, XIII and von Willebrand factor
opts.why: Cryoprecipitate contains fibrinogen (I), VIII, XIII and vWF.

questions.expl: Cryo is concentrated fibrinogen, FVIII, FXIII, vWF and fibronectin; local dosing and fibrinogen concentrate availability vary.

questions.stem: Three-factor prothrombin complex concentrate reverses warfarin therapy within

opts.why: Too delayed; vitamin K takes hours, PCC works rapidly.
PCC rapidly supplies vitamin-K dependent factors to reverse warfarin effect.
Not the PCC onset.
Not applicable to factor replacement.

questions.expl: Three-factor PCC (II, IX, X) works within minutes, though 4-factor PCC plus IV vitamin K is commonly preferred for urgent warfarin reversal today.

questions.stem: The difference between a size 5.0 microlaryngeal tube (MLT) and a standard size 5.0 endotracheal tube is that the size 5 MLT

opts.t: The MLT has a 7.0-mm internal diameter
opts.why: Its listed size 5.0 is its ID.
Adult MLT variants are cuffed.

opts.t: The MLT has a shorter shaft
opts.why: Opposite of its design.
Same 5.0-mm internal diameter but designed longer for laryngeal surgery.

questions.expl: MLT is a long, narrow-bore endotracheal tube providing surgical access to larynx while keeping cuff distal; anticipate higher flow resistance.

questions.stem: A third heart sound at the apex may be heard in

opts.why: Physiological S3 may be audible due to increased ventricular filling/flow.
Usually produces right-sided findings rather than physiological S3 at LV apex.
Typically a friction rub, not a physiological S3.
Classically ejection systolic murmur/click.

questions.expl: An S3 at apex can be normal in children, young adults and pregnancy; in older adults it may suggest volume overload or ventricular failure.

questions.stem: Consideration for same-day discharge in an ex-premature infant after orchidopexy for undescended testis would be suitable at a minimum postmenstrual age of

opts.why: Too young given former prematurity/apnoea risk.
Cited minimum for healthy term infant, not ex-premature.
ANZCA guidance for healthy ex-premature infant considered for same-day discharge.
Less than the guidance for ex-premature day case.

questions.expl: Former premature infants are at risk of postoperative apnoea; ANZCA PG29 specifies around 54 weeks PMA with appropriate clinical assessment.

questions.stem: A feature that is atypical of multiple sclerosis is

opts.why: Common demyelinating symptom.
Common from internuclear ophthalmoplegia/brainstem lesions.
Common MS manifestations.
Cortical language deficit is distinctly atypical for classical multiple sclerosis presentations.

questions.expl: Multiple sclerosis classically affects optic nerves, spinal cord and brainstem white matter, causing visual, sensory and motor signs; isolated aphasia is relatively unusual.

questions.stem: A patient with severe abdominal trauma develops acute respiratory distress syndrome. A diagnosis of abdominal compartment syndrome is confirmed if the patient also has a sustained intraabdominal pressure greater than

opts.why: Below IAH threshold and insufficient.

opts.t: Intra-abdominal pressure >20 mmHg with new organ dysfunction
opts.why: Defines abdominal compartment syndrome.
Defines intra-abdominal hypertension, not ACS.
Insufficient without new organ dysfunction.

questions.expl: WSACS defines ACS as sustained IAP >20 mmHg associated with new organ dysfunction/failure; a positive pressure threshold alone is insufficient.

questions.stem: The tip of an ideally-placed intra-aortic balloon catheter should lie in the

opts.why: Wrong position and potentially hazardous.
Too low for effective counterpulsation and risks visceral/renal circulation.

opts.t: 2–3 cm distal to the left subclavian artery origin
opts.why: IABP tip belongs in proximal descending thoracic aorta below LSCA.
Not the correct arterial placement.

questions.expl: Correct femoral IABP position: radiopaque tip ~2 cm below left subclavian artery, distal end above renal arteries.

questions.stem: Tranexamic acid is NOT useful for managing

opts.why: WOMAN trial supports early TXA to reduce death due to bleeding.
CRASH-2 supports early administration in selected patients.
HALT-IT found no survival benefit and increased seizures/thromboembolic events with TXA.
TXA reduces transfusion in many cardiac surgical settings.

questions.expl: Do not routinely use TXA in GI haemorrhage after large HALT-IT trial; weigh indication-specific evidence for trauma/PPH/cardiac surgery.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old woman is administered a nerve block for extraction of her right lower wisdom tooth. The nerve that should be blocked is the

opts.why: Terminal branch supplies lower lip/chin, not molar pulpal anaesthesia.
Maxillary upper dentition/face.
Supplies lower mandibular molars and teeth via mandibular canal.
Posterior hard palate rather than lower wisdom tooth.

questions.expl: Mandibular third molar extraction requires inferior alveolar block, with lingual/long buccal supplementation as appropriate.

questions.stem: An adult patient undergoing surgical aortic valve replacement is in ventricular fibrillation after the removal of the aortic cross clamp and requires internal defibrillation. It has been shown it is safe to deliver a charge of up to

opts.why: Recalled internal paddles maximum 'safe' upper charge around 50 J, though typical first doses are substantially lower.
Generally insufficient for adult internal defibrillation.
Standard external monophasic-equivalent energy, excessive internally.
External-defibrillation energy, not appropriate internally.

questions.expl: Internal defibrillation through direct paddles usually starts around 10–20 J; energies up to ~50 J can be used in adult operating theatre protocols.

opts.why: Preductal saturation allows assessment before ductal mixing.
Postductal site.
Postductal site.

opts.why: Not for early transitional preductal assessment.

questions.expl: For newborn resuscitation preductal oximetry goes on right hand/wrist; early SpO2 targets differ from older children/adults.

questions.stem: The causes of macrocytic anaemia include

opts.why: Typically microcytic.
Alcohol can cause macrocytosis and macrocytic anaemia.
Usually microcytic.
Usually normocytic or microcytic.

questions.expl: Other macrocytosis causes include B12/folate deficiency, liver disease, hypothyroidism, marrow disorders and some drugs; among recalled options, alcohol is classic.

questions.stem: The function of the (electrical) earth conductor in operating theatre patient monitoring equipment is to

opts.t: Protective earthing to prevent electric shock from exposed equipment casing
opts.why: Earth provides a low-resistance fault path permitting protective device disconnection.

opts.t: To guarantee prevention of all microshock
opts.why: Microshock risk requires additional isolation and leakage-current measures.

opts.t: To supply normal mains power to equipment
opts.why: Live/neutral conduct power.
Not its electrical safety purpose.

questions.expl: Protective earth conducts fault current and promotes tripping of safety devices, reducing macroshock/electrocution risk.

questions.stem: The next patient on your endoscopy list is a 50-year-old woman who has been scheduled for gastroscopy and colonoscopy under sedation, after unsatisfactory proceduralist-supervised midazolam and fentanyl sedation in the past. She states that she has egg anaphylaxis and carries an adrenaline (epinephrine) auto-injector. The most appropriate agent to use for her sedation is

opts.why: Egg allergy is not a routine contraindication to propofol in adults; emulsifier egg lecithin lacks the relevant egg proteins.

opts.t: Ketamine solely because of egg allergy
opts.why: May be a sedative alternative but allergy alone does not mandate substitution.

opts.t: Sevoflurane inhalational sedation as first choice
opts.why: Not necessary for typical endoscopy.
Opioid does not provide adequate hypnosis for endoscopy.

questions.expl: Published allergy reviews show propofol is generally safe in egg/soy/peanut allergy, including most egg anaphylaxis histories; assess prior actual reaction to propofol.
questions.note: Exam/evidence qualification: Anaesthetic drug choice for ECT depends on seizure duration and haemodynamic needs; interpretation depends on recalled options.

questions.stem: During standard diagnostic nocturnal polysomnography for investigation of obstructive sleep apnoea, apnoea is defined as cessation of airflow for

opts.why: Too short.
Too short for adult polysomnographic definition.
Standard sleep-lab apnoea definition requires marked airflow reduction for ≥10 sec.
Longer than necessary.

questions.expl: Apnoea in adults: ≥90% airflow reduction for ≥10 seconds on a diagnostic study; paediatric event duration may use breaths criteria.

questions.stem: A healthy woman is admitted to the obstetric unit with threatened preterm labour at 29 weeks gestation. Her blood pressure is 140/80 mmHg. A magnesium sulfate infusion is indicated for the purpose of

opts.t: Direct suppression of maternal hypertension alone
opts.why: Not primary reason in normotensive threatened preterm labour.
MgSO4 in threatened very preterm birth reduces risk of cerebral palsy in surviving infants.
Corticosteroids are used for this.
Magnesium is not given to stimulate labour.

questions.expl: At 29 weeks threatened preterm delivery, magnesium sulphate is administered for fetal neuroprotection, following local gestational-age criteria.

questions.stem: You are asked to review a 5-year-old child weighing 24 kg in the recovery room for acute pain management after a tonsillectomy performed for obstructive sleep apnoea. The most appropriate analgesic regimen would be

opts.why: Codeine is contraindicated after paediatric adenotonsillectomy due to unpredictable morphine exposure and respiratory depression.
Risk of opioid-induced ventilatory impairment in OSA.
Bleeding risk and not standard for children.

opts.t: Regular paracetamol plus ibuprofen, with cautious rescue opioid if needed
opts.why: Multimodal non-opioid baseline analgesia is favoured after tonsillectomy, especially with OSA.

questions.expl: PROSPECT recommends paracetamol+NSAID and dexamethasone, with opioids as rescue; use special caution in children with OSA.

questions.stem: The bioavailability of an oral dose of ketamine is approximately

opts.why: Oral ketamine has extensive first-pass metabolism and low bioavailability.
More consistent with routes avoiding first pass.
Much higher than usual oral exposure.
Would imply no first-pass loss.

questions.expl: Oral ketamine bioavailability ≈17–25%, versus higher parenteral/intranasal routes; norketamine production is substantial.

questions.stem: A patient presents for a transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP). He had a single drug-eluting coronary stent for angina pectoris inserted six months ago and is taking clopidogrel and aspirin. The most appropriate preoperative management of his medications is to

opts.t: Stop clopidogrel 5 days before, continue aspirin
opts.why: With six-month-old DES and surgery proceeding, this is recalled standard strategy after cardiology risk assessment.
Reverses preferred perioperative antiplatelet strategy.
Increases stent thrombosis risk.

opts.t: Continue dual therapy without discussing TURP bleeding risk
opts.why: TURP can bleed significantly; individualise multidisciplinary decisions.

questions.expl: After elective DES at six months, historical guideline allows surgery with aspirin continued and clopidogrel interrupted ~5 days when necessary. Updated stent guidance and very-high-bleed procedures require cardiology consultation.

questions.stem: Of the following, the drug that is LEAST likely to provide effective analgesia following paediatric tonsillectomy is

opts.why: Evidence-based core postoperative analgesic.
Evidence-based core analgesic unless contraindicated.
Volatile agents provide hypnosis/immobility but are not an effective postoperative analgesic strategy.
Has demonstrated analgesic benefits after tonsillectomy.

questions.expl: This stem's recalled option sets conflict. The chosen reconstructed options make volatile anaesthesia the clear least-effective analgesic; if actual alternatives differ (e.g. clonidine/remifentanil), the original intended answer is not certain.
questions.note: Exam/evidence qualification: Recall sources disagree on the original choices. The working key is correct for the four reconstructed options, not a certified ANZCA original option.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old woman on aspirin therapy presents to her ophthalmologist for follow up three days after you performed a transconjunctival peribulbar block for cataract surgery on her left eye. She complains of painless periorbital swelling, erythema and mild chemosis which started the day after surgery but is improving. She also had a peribulbar block three weeks ago for surgery on the other eye. The most likely diagnosis is

opts.why: Usually painful, tender and progressive with fever/orbital features.
Typically acute painful tense orbit, proptosis and visual compromise.
Painless resolving superficial bruising after peribulbar block in aspirin patient fits this.
Would be acute systemic onset, not local improving bruising days later.

questions.expl: Recalled presentation suggests benign local bleeding after block rather than orbital compartment syndrome or infection; verify vision/IOP if clinically concerned.

questions.stem: This 12 lead ECG shows

opts.t: Left posterior fascicular block with RBBB
opts.why: Typically produces right axis rather than left axis deviation.
Requires independent atrial and ventricular rhythms, not just bifascicular morphology.

opts.t: Right bundle branch block with left anterior fascicular block
opts.why: Branscape recalled ECG showed RBBB plus left axis deviation, forming bifascicular block.
Progressive PR prolongation and dropped beats, not the key ECG finding.

questions.expl: The recalled Brainscape answer is RBBB + LAFB, but original exam ECG is unavailable. A representative teaching diagram should not be represented as the actual exam tracing.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old woman has critical bleeding following major trauma. Her blood group is unknown. Fresh frozen plasma that she receives should ideally be from

opts.why: Contains anti-A and anti-B antibodies, unsuitable universally.
Can contain anti-A antibodies.
Contains anti-B and may be used as a low-titre emergency alternative under some current protocols, but AB is classically compatible with all recipients.
Contains neither anti-A nor anti-B, making AB the universal plasma donor group.

questions.expl: For unknown recipient blood group, group AB FFP is traditional universal plasma; many services use validated low-titre group A in emergencies because AB supply is limited.

questions.stem: The success rate of stopping smoking before surgery is NOT improved by

opts.why: Evidence-based cessation aid.
Evidence-based cessation aid.
Not proven smoking-cessation pharmacotherapy.
Has some evidence for smoking cessation though not first-line.

questions.expl: ANZCA smoking cessation background evidence supports varenicline and bupropion, with some evidence for nortriptyline/clonidine; SSRIs are not effective quit aids.

questions.stem: A woman who is to undergo a caesarean section reports that she is allergic to amoxicillin. The reaction is limited to a rash. For surgical antimicrobial prophylaxis, you should administer

opts.why: Not standard caesarean surgical prophylaxis.
Insufficient as standard first-line and used with additional gram-negative cover for severe β-lactam allergy.
Non-severe delayed rash to amoxicillin generally does not preclude cefazolin perioperative prophylaxis.
Caesarean prophylaxis reduces endometritis/wound infection.

questions.expl: Give IV cefazolin for usual non-severe penicillin rash; severe immediate reactions require local alternative regimens and allergy assessment.

questions.stem: Compared to a continuous epidural infusion, patient controlled epidural analgesia does NOT reduce

opts.why: PCEA may reduce total consumption.
PCEA does not reliably reduce caesarean rate relative to continuous infusion.
May be reduced with PCEA/PIEB techniques.
Some automated/PCEA programmes reduce clinician top-ups.

questions.expl: PCEA provides effective labour analgesia, can reduce dose and motor block while obstetric outcomes, including CS rates, remain broadly similar.

questions.stem: The use of erythropoietin before major surgery results in

opts.why: Contradicts meta-analysis.

opts.t: Lower allogeneic RBC transfusion requirements, without demonstrated increase in thrombosis in studied populations
opts.why: Cochrane evidence supports rHuEPO plus iron reducing transfusion in selected anaemic surgery patients.

opts.t: Uniform increase in thrombosis in all trials
opts.why: Evidence is not that categorical, though thrombotic precautions matter.
Not established.

questions.expl: Pre-op erythropoietin plus iron can improve haemoglobin and reduce transfusion; weigh thrombosis risk and appropriateness. Benefits not universal in all surgical settings.
questions.note: Exam/evidence qualification: Erythropoietin may reduce red cell transfusion; thromboembolic risks must be considered and evidence varies.

questions.stem: Anaesthesia-induced rhabdomyolysis differs from malignant hyperthermia in that it is NOT

opts.why: Typical AIR lacks the marked hypermetabolic ETCO₂ rise of MH.
AIR generally lacks MH-like sustained rigidity.

opts.t: Reduced myoglobinaemia compared with malignant hyperthermia
opts.why: This is NOT a reliable difference: both may cause major myoglobin release.
Distinguishes AIR from classic MH.

questions.expl: Anaesthesia-induced rhabdomyolysis and MH both may cause hyperkalaemia/myoglobin release; AIR lacks the archetypal sustained hypermetabolism and rigidity.

questions.stem: Of the following, the drug which is most effective in the management of severe hyperthermia in serotonergic syndrome is

opts.why: Antipyretics do not treat muscle-generated hyperthermia.
No established role for serotonin-syndrome heat production.

opts.t: Rocuronium with deep sedation and ventilation
opts.why: In severe serotonin-syndrome hyperthermia from muscular activity, nondepolarising paralysis rapidly stops heat production.
Benzodiazepines are first-line for agitation/mild disease but may be insufficient in extreme hyperthermia.

questions.expl: For severe hyperthermia (e.g. >41°C) due to serotonin syndrome, intubation, deep sedation and non-depolarising NMB are key; avoid succinylcholine with possible hyperkalaemia.
questions.note: Exam/evidence qualification: The drug addresses dangerous muscle activity/heat generation; it is not specific serotonin-receptor antagonism.

questions.stem: In order to minimise the risk of cardiac arrhythmia, surgical diathermy has been designed to operate with

opts.why: Above neuromuscular stimulation frequency, diathermy produces heating with reduced arrhythmia risk.
Can stimulate nerves/myocardium.
Not the standard electrosurgery design.

opts.t: Low-frequency pulses to maximize muscle activation
opts.why: Opposite of safety goal.

questions.expl: Electrosurgery uses radiofrequency high-frequency current (hundreds of kHz to MHz) to generate heating while avoiding low-frequency neuromuscular stimulation.

questions.stem: The medication most strongly associated with an acute primary hypotensive reaction following transfusion of blood products is

opts.why: ACE inhibition reduces bradykinin breakdown, predisposing to isolated hypotensive transfusion reactions.
β blockade not the characteristic bradykinin mechanism.
Does not inhibit bradykinin degradation in the same way.
Vasodilator but not characteristic risk medication for AHTR.

questions.expl: Acute hypotensive transfusion reactions are often bradykinin mediated; ACE inhibitors impair bradykinin degradation and increase susceptibility.
